sources.citation: Lloyd N. Trefethen, Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice, SIAM, 2013, author-hosted first-six-chapter sample.
sources.format: Public author-hosted PDF sample; extracted locally with Python 3 / PyMuPDF (fitz).
sources.rights_note: Copyrighted author sample; no open licence is asserted. The complete sample cache is kept only in ignored scratchpad/.
sources.read_status: Complete for the substantive sample content, printed Chapters 2–6, physical PDF pp. 14–55. Front matter pp. 1–13 and the book beyond this sample were not read.
read_ranges: Chapter 2: polynomial interpolation at distinct nodes and Chebyshev points; uniqueness is stated as known rather than proved.
Chapter 3: Chebyshev polynomials/series and aliasing; the series proof imports a standard Fourier/Laurent result.
Chapter 4: Chebyshev coefficients and aliasing examples.
Chapter 5: barycentric interpolation formula and its proof.
Chapter 6: Weierstrass approximation theorem proof outline by Gaussian smoothing and entire-function/Taylor approximation; later Runge/Lebesgue convergence chapters are outside this sample.
proof_limits: The sample does not supply the Lagrange interpolation remainder theorem or a full proof of the Chebyshev Lebesgue-constant estimate.
The Weierstrass argument is an outline and assumes imported Fourier/Laurent facts; it is not recorded as a complete locally importable proof.

sources.citation: Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, SIAM, 2017, author-hosted online textbook pages.
sources.format: Public author-hosted HTML textbook articles converted from their visible article body to local PDFs and extracted text with PyMuPDF (fitz).
sources.rights_note: Copyrighted book pages; no open licence is asserted. Source HTML, local PDFs, and full extraction stay in ignored scratchpad/.
sources.read_status: Complete for the six listed article bodies; the book and website outside them were not read.

read_ranges.scope_notes: Vandermonde interpolation computation and polynomial interpolation demos; not a full interpolation-remainder or convergence proof.
Sections 5.6 and related article material: composite trapezoid from piecewise-linear interpolation, second-order error, Euler–Maclaurin/extrapolation and Simpson context; not Gaussian quadrature.
Adaptive Simpson/Richardson error indicator and counterexample showing a requested tolerance is not a certified error guarantee.
Embedded error estimates and step control; tolerance is a target, not a general guarantee. The referenced fixed-step order theorem was not read in this article.
Conditioning versus algorithm choice and consequences for interpolation and polynomial bases.
Relative rounding model, unit roundoff, IEEE ranges and exceptions; page read as context, not a new library supplier.

proof_limits: The interpolation article demonstrates numerical computation, not the full interpolation remainder or Lebesgue stability proofs.
The adaptive integration estimator is explicitly heuristic and has a counterexample to the claimed tolerance as a guarantee.
The adaptive RK chapter does not prove a generic convergence/error theorem.

sources.citation: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, author-hosted book and chapter PDFs, copyright dates 2009–2023.
sources.format: Public author-hosted PDF chapters; extracted with PyMuPDF (fitz).
sources.rights_note: Each chapter page states: “do not distribute or post electronically without author’s permission.” Copies and extractions remain only in ignored scratchpad/; tracked citations and summaries contain no copied chapter text.
sources.read_status: Complete for quadrature Ch. 7 and the main text, end notes, and exercises of Practical QMC Chs. 15 and 17; selected Simple Monte Carlo sections only. Other downloaded chapters are not represented as read.

read_ranges.read_ranges: §§2.1–2.3 and §2.9, printed pp. 15–21 and 35–36; physical PDF pp. 16–22 and 36–37. Other sections, end-note details, and exercises were not read.
read_ranges.proof_limits: The IID CLT is stated with finite variance and positive variance, but the proof is cited to Chung (1974). Hoeffding’s inequality is stated with bounded independent variables, but its proof is cited elsewhere. The sample-variance estimator and variance identity are elementary and derivable locally.

read_ranges.read_ranges: Full 36-page extracted chapter body, including end notes and exercises.
read_ranges.proof_limits: The midpoint error proof and composite rules are developed in the chapter. Gaussian quadrature exactness/error, Bakhvalov results, and Laplace-method results are stated with external proof references rather than proved there.

read_ranges.read_ranges: Full main text §§15.1–15.8, physical PDF pp. 11–72 (printed pp. 9–70), chapter end notes and exercises; the full extraction was read after filtering only 23 figure-artifact lines longer than 1,200 characters, none prose/theorem lines.
read_ranges.proof_limits: The one-dimensional summation-by-parts theorem proof is supplied. Uniform-distribution convergence and Koksma–Hlawka are cited to exercises or external sources; digital-net discrepancy rates and higher-order net results are mostly cited, not proved. Koksma–Hlawka requires finite Hardy–Krause variation and gives no generally usable empirical error bar because discrepancy and variation are normally unknown.

read_ranges.chapter: Practical QMC, Chapter 17, Randomized quasi-Monte Carlo
read_ranges.read_ranges: Full main text §§17.1–17.14, physical PDF pp. 103–157 (printed pp. 101–155), chapter end notes and exercises, physical PDF pp. 155–160 (printed pp. 153–158). Appendices and later chapters were not read as part of this chapter review.
read_ranges.proof_limits: Unbiasedness follows from pointwise uniform marginals. The nested uniform scramble variance theorem for (0,m,d)-nets (Theorem 17.3) is sourced to Owen (1997a); smooth-net variance rates, RQMC CLTs and singular-integrand bounds also cite external proofs. The book warns that randomized replicates estimate randomization variation, not data-sampling uncertainty; CLT/calibration requires additional assumptions and may be poor for small replicate counts.

not_read_as_full_text: Practical QMC appendices A–C, the remainder of the bibliography, and the rest of the book.
Downloaded Ch. 1 Introduction outside the stated Ch. 2 ranges, Ch. 8 variance reduction, Ch. 9 importance sampling, and Ch. 11 MCMC are not claimed as read in this dossier.

sources.citation: Michael B. Giles, “Multilevel Monte Carlo Path Simulation,” Operations Research 56(3) (2008), 607–617.
sources.format: Public author-hosted paper PDF; entire 11-page paper and full extracted text read.
sources.rights_note: Publisher copyright applies; author-hosted copy used for research, full cache only in ignored scratchpad/.
sources.read_ranges: Full paper, especially §2 multilevel estimator and §3 Theorem 3.1 with proof, PDF pp. 1–11.
sources.proof_limits: The abstract complexity theorem is proved. The paper does not prove general SDE weak/strong convergence rates; the Euler payoff example imports those rates. Its adaptive level/bias stopping rule is presented as a practical heuristic, not a guaranteed error bound.

sources.citation: Desmond J. Higham, Xuerong Mao, and Andrew M. Stuart, “Strong Convergence of Euler-Type Methods for Nonlinear Stochastic Differential Equations,” SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 40(3) (2002), 1041–1063.
sources.format: Public author-repository paper PDF; extracted with PyMuPDF (fitz).
sources.rights_note: Publisher copyright applies; author repository copy used as evidence. Full source cache remains in ignored scratchpad/.
sources.read_status: Read journal pp. 1041–1056, PDF pp. 1–16, including Theorem 2.2 and proof and the optimal-rate Theorem 4.4 and proof. Remaining pp. 1057–1063 / PDF pp. 17–23, including implicit methods, were not read.
proof_limits: Theorem 2.2 is a qualitative strong mean-square supremum convergence result under local Lipschitz assumptions plus finite p>2 sup moments for the exact solution and EM interpolation; it gives no rate.

Theorem 4.4 gives the optimal mean-square supremum order O(h) only for autonomous C¹ drift/diffusion, one-sided-Lipschitz drift, globally Lipschitz diffusion, polynomial local-Lipschitz drift, and uniform finite moments of every order for the exact solution, step process, and continuous interpolation.
This article proves no weak-order-1 theorem. Its assumptions do not justify a time-dependent extension without a separate result.

sources.citation: Simo Särkkä and Arno Solin, Applied Stochastic Differential Equations, Cambridge University Press, 2019; Aalto-hosted author PDF.
sources.format: Public author-hosted book PDF; full Chapter 8 extracted with PyMuPDF (fitz).
sources.rights_note: Copyrighted Cambridge book; no open licence is asserted here. Full cached copy is kept in ignored scratchpad/.
sources.read_status: Complete Chapter 8 §§8.1–8.9, printed pp. 126–164, PDF pp. 145–173; no other chapter is claimed as read.
sources.scope_notes: Itô and Itô–Taylor methods, Euler–Maruyama/Milstein, strong and weak error definitions, stochastic Runge–Kutta and Verlet methods.
sources.proof_limits: The preface explicitly prioritizes readable exposition over full measure-theoretic rigor. Strong order 1/2 and weak order 1 are stated under ‘sufficient regularity’ and cited to Kloeden–Platen; derivations are informal and do not provide exact theorem hypotheses or a full proof. Context only, not an import for the local weak theorem design.

sources.citation: Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Cambridge University Press, 2004; author-hosted Stanford PDF.
sources.format: Public author-hosted full textbook PDF; selected Chapter 9 sections extracted and read.
sources.rights_note: Copyrighted book; author-hosted access is not treated as a reuse licence. Full downloaded cache stays only in ignored scratchpad/.
sources.read_status: Read §9.2 and §9.3.1 (physical PDF pp. 477–483, printed pp. 463–469) and §§9.5.1–9.5.3 (physical PDF pp. 498–506, printed pp. 484–492), including the full line-search, strong-convex gradient, and damped-Newton proofs. §9.3.2 examples beyond its opening and all other Chapter 9 sections and textbook chapters were not read.
read_ranges: §9.2 and §9.3.1: descent direction and Armijo backtracking termination; gradient-descent exact/backtracking linear objective-gap rate under mI ≼ ∇²f ≼ MI on the initial sublevel set. The §9.3.2 examples were not read beyond their opening context.

§§9.5.1–9.5.3: Newton step/decrement, damped Newton, and convergence proof under C² strong convexity and an L-Lipschitz Hessian on the sublevel set; finite damped phase followed by full Newton steps and quadratic convergence.
sources.proof_limits: These convex regimes do not prove a global convergence theorem for arbitrary nonconvex likelihoods or identify a global maximum in a multimodal statistical model.

sources.citation: Per Christian Hansen, 02906 Introduction to Inverse Problems, DTU author-hosted lecture slides, chapters 3–8 and 12.
sources.format: Public university/author-hosted lecture-slide PDFs; extracted with PyMuPDF (fitz).
sources.rights_note: Author-hosted lecture material; no open licence is asserted. Full downloaded slide PDFs and text remain only in ignored scratchpad/.
sources.read_status: Complete for Ch. 4 Regularization Methods (all 29 slides) and Ch. 5 Regularization Parameter Choice (all 27 slides); Ch. 3 Discretization pp. 1–6 read as context. Other downloaded chapters are not claimed as read.
sources.scope_notes: Discrete ill-conditioning, TSVD/Tikhonov filter factors, bias-versus-data-perturbation decomposition, and parameter-selection heuristics (discrepancy principle, L-curve, GCV, normalized cumulative periodogram). sources.proof_limits: These slide decks are pedagogical context and examples, not complete proof sources for the current library’s published least-squares or Tikhonov items. L-curve, GCV, discrepancy and NCP rules are choices/heuristics with model-specific limits, not universal regularization-parameter guarantees.
